opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the big takeaway for me was that the gap between "the model knows a lot about biology" and "the model can actually help someone do biology" was closing faster than a lot of us expected. With protocol and wet-lab style tasks, you're not just testing recall. You're testing whether the model can troubleshoot, notice when a step is going to fail, and reason about what's actually happening in the tube. Seeing early reasoning models do well there was a signal that these systems are starting to do something that looks like practical scientific judgment.

For the next generation of evals, that has a few implications. First, a lot of our existing benchmarks are going to saturate, if they haven't already. Multiple-choice questions, even really hard expert-written ones, just don't have enough headroom. So we have to move toward tasks that are longer-horizon and more open-ended, where the model has to plan an experiment, interpret messy results, and iterate, closer to what a real researcher does over days or weeks rather than in one answer.

Second, we need evals that are grounded in reality. It's one thing to grade a written protocol, and another to ask whether following that protocol actually works when someone does it at the bench. Getting closer to real-world outcomes, whether through collaborations with labs or carefully designed uplift studies, is going to matter a lot, because that's what tells you whether the capability is real.

And third, there's a dual-use side we have to take seriously. The same capability that could speed up drug discovery or help a grad student debug a failed experiment could also give uplift in areas we really care about from a safety perspective. So the evals have to do double duty: measure the beneficial capabilities we want to push forward, and also give us early warning on the risky ones so the safeguards are in place before the capability arrives, not after.

So I'd say it raised the bar. It told us we need to build evals that look much more like actual science, and we need to build them ahead of where the models are, because they're catching up quickly.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest lesson wasn't about the model, it was about the evaluation itself.

When we designed that eval, the goal was to get past the thing that had been bugging us for a while, which is that most of our science benchmarks were really measuring recall or textbook reasoning. You ask a model a question with a known answer, you grade it, you get a number. That's useful, but it tells you very little about whether a model can actually help a scientist do work. So the protein-synthesis eval was an attempt to close that gap. We had the model write out protocols, troubleshoot, make choices about reagents and conditions, and then real people in a real lab executed those protocols and reported back what happened. The thing being graded was whether the experiment worked, not whether the answer matched a key.

And what surprised us was two things. First, the early reasoning model did meaningfully better than we expected, especially on the troubleshooting side, where something goes wrong mid-protocol and you have to reason about why. Second, and this is the part I keep coming back to, the places it failed were almost never the places our paper benchmarks would have predicted. It would nail the conceptual question and then suggest a step that any grad student would know is impractical, or it would underweight some piece of tacit knowledge that never shows up in the literature because nobody writes it down.

So what does that imply going forward? A few things.

One, I think the next generation of scientific evals has to be grounded in outcomes in the world, not just correctness on paper. That's expensive. Wet-lab evals are slow, they're noisy, you have to think hard about how to make them reproducible and how to separate model error from experimental variance. But I don't think there's a shortcut. If we want to make claims like "this model accelerates science," we need measurements that are actually about science getting done.

Two, we need to measure the whole loop, not a single step. Real research is iterative. You propose something, it half-works, you update. Most evals today are one-shot. The interesting signal is in how a model behaves across that loop, and whether it gets better or worse as information comes back.

Three, and this is the one I feel most strongly about, these evals have to be built with domain experts in the room from day one. Not as graders after the fact, but as co-designers. The failure modes that matter are the ones only a practitioner would think to test for.

And then the last piece is the safety dimension, which for biology is unavoidable. Capability on something like protein synthesis is dual-use by nature. So part of what the result implies for us is that the eval program and the safety program can't be separate tracks. The same measurements that tell you a model is becoming genuinely useful to a biologist are the ones telling you where you need mitigations. We treat that as one problem, not two.

So I'd summarize it as: the early success was encouraging, but what it really did was validate the methodology. It showed that you can build evaluations that are real enough to be trusted, and that when you do, you learn things you couldn't have learned any other way. The next generation should take that seriously and push much further into the actual practice of science.

astra-6.text:
I think it suggests that our evaluations need to move closer to the actual practice of science. Answering a question correctly is one thing; helping someone carry out an experiment successfully is another. A wet-lab evaluation can start to measure that gap.

For the next generation, I’d want to understand how a model handles the whole experimental process: choosing an approach, interpreting results, troubleshooting when something fails, and knowing when the evidence isn’t sufficient. And we need to test across different settings, because success on one protein-synthesis task doesn’t establish broad scientific capability.

There’s also a safety dimension. As models become more useful in real experiments, evaluations need to measure both the scientific benefits they enable and the risks that come with those capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it suggests that the next generation of scientific evaluations needs to measure more than whether a model can give a convincing answer. We need to understand whether its advice actually helps someone carry out a scientific task in the real world.

For a wet-lab evaluation, that means looking at the whole process: Can the model help design an experiment, interpret results, and troubleshoot when something goes wrong? And how much does that assistance improve performance compared with what someone could do without it?

I’d also be careful about generalizing from success on one task. You want evaluations across different tasks and levels of user expertise, with enough repetition to distinguish a reliable capability from a one-off result. That gives us a better picture of both the scientific value and the risks as these models improve.
